title: Sign legibility is arithmetic — Image Wiki
text:
Sign legibility is arithmetic
  How big, how thick, how far apart, how much contrast. Most of it is calculated from viewing distance and mounting height, and the legal numbers are floors rather than goals.

  
    Termsign legibility
    Also calledcharacter height, sign contrast, ADA sign requirements
    Not the same ascomprehension, readability of long text, brand typography
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Height comes from distanceWhy all-caps hurts at distanceContrast, and an honest gap in the lawThese are floors, not targetsCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Stand at a hospital reception desk and try to read the room numbers on the far wall. If you cannot, it is not because the designer had poor taste. Someone picked a letter height without measuring the distance from the desk to the wall — and a sign nobody can read is a hole in the wayfinding whatever else is right about it.
Almost everything about whether a sign can be read is calculated. Two site measurements — how far away the reader is stuck, and how high the sign is mounted — set the minimum letter height. Stroke width and spacing then follow as percentages of that height. The numbers below are the ones a US inspector actually checks.
Height comes from distance
The ADA Standards make minimum character height a stepped function of two things: the height of the characters above the floor, and the horizontal viewing distance — the distance from the character to whatever obstruction stops you getting closer. A counter, a rail, a planter, the edge of a platform.

Left, the two numbers you measure on site. Note that the viewing distance is set by the obstruction, not by where people happen to stand — if a counter holds you 20 feet back, 20 feet is the number.
Right, what the rule then produces. Each band is flat up to a knee and then climbs at one eighth of an inch per additional foot. Follow the accent line: a sign at normal eye level read from 20 feet behind a counter needs characters 2 3/8 inches high, not the 5/8 inch that satisfies a corridor doorplate. The three lines converge because a high sign starts big but grows at the same rate.


Everything else is a ratio of that cap height:



Quantity
ADA requirement




Stroke thickness, visual characters
10–30% of cap height


Stroke thickness, raised characters
15% maximum


Character width (cap O vs cap I)
55–110%


Space between characters
10–35% of cap height


Space between lines
135–170% of cap height


Raised character height
1/2″ – 2″ (5/8″ min if also read visually)


Tactile characters above the floor
48″ min to 60″ max, at the baselines


Visual characters above the floor
40″ min


Clear headroom under an overhead sign
80″ min



Two of those repay a second look. Stroke thickness has an upper bound, because too thick a stroke closes up the counters of a, e and o until letters become blobs — heavy is not legible. And the tactile band, 48 to 60 inches, is set by the height of a hand: the one dimension on the sign that has nothing to do with looking.



Photo: Eddau, 2007, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
A room sign built to the pattern: raised sans-serif capitals, Grade 2 braille directly under each line of characters, and the pictogram field kept clear of both. The raised characters must be uppercase — a rule about fingertips rather than eyes, since a tactile reader tracks a constant-height band. Note also that the braille is not required to contrast with the plate, only the visual and raised characters are.


Why all-caps hurts at distance
For characters read with the eyes, the ADA allows upper case, lower case, or a mix. Everyone who designs for distance picks the mix, and Legible London says why in one line: upper and lower case wherever possible, for maximum legibility.
The mechanism is word shape. Ascenders and descenders give a lower-case word a distinctive silhouette — hospital has a tall h and l, a dotted i, a descending p — and that outline survives when the letters themselves have gone soft, from distance, motion, dim light or peripheral vision. Set the same word in capitals and every glyph is the same height: the outline is a rectangle, so the reader resolves letters one at a time. Capitals also run wider, eating the panel you needed for a bigger cap height.
Caps are not banned. They earn their place on short, learned messages where nobody reads a word shape anyway.



Photo: Hugh Llewelyn, Oval Underground Station (Northern Line), 2025, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
Two words, all capitals, white on dark blue vitreous enamel — and it works, because WAY OUT is a fixed phrase you recognise as a shape and never actually read. The arrow carries as much of the message as the words. Note the finish: enamel is glossy but the panel sits flat on a wall lit from the platform, and TfL's standards handle the remaining risk by controlling sightlines instead — exclusion zones around signs so departure indicators cannot block them, and repeater signs where the distance is too great.


Contrast, and an honest gap in the law
The ADA is specific about geometry and vague about contrast. It requires characters to contrast with their background as either light-on-dark or dark-on-light with a non-glare finish, and then declines to name a number.
The Access Board explains why, and the explanation is worth more than a number: contrast is based on a colour's light reflectance value, LRV, normally measured with a spectrophotometer, and measuring LRV accurately in the field is difficult — affected by the sign's materials and by the lighting. A rule you cannot enforce on site gets ignored, so they wrote down the part checkable by eye.
British practice does give the number. RNIB, quoting BS 8300, asks for a difference of at least 20 LRV points between adjacent critical surfaces, with 30 preferred, valid where the surfaces are lit to 200 lux or more. LRV runs from 0 to 99: the higher, the lighter. It is value, measured — lightness alone, with the hue thrown away.

WARD 6letters LRV 42.7 · plate LRV 47.0WARD 6the same two colours, colour removed4 points apartfails: the letters sink into the plateWARD 6letters LRV 25.7 · plate LRV 47.0WARD 6the same two colours, colour removed21 points apartclears the 20-point floor, only justWARD 6letters LRV 4.6 · plate LRV 47.0WARD 6the same two colours, colour removed42 points apartpast the 30 points RNIB prefers

One plate colour, three letter colours, and the only variable is the letters' LRV. Underneath each pair is the same combination with the colour stripped out.
Left, four points apart: legible-ish in colour, gone in grey. Middle, 21 points — over the BS 8300 floor and no further. Right, 42 points, which is what a sign you can read across a lobby looks like. This is why RNIB warns against relying on hue: two colours as different as green and brown can sit within a few points of each other, and a person with low vision or colour vision deficiency sees the grey version.


The lux condition matters as much as the LRV. Contrast perception falls at low light levels, so RNIB asks for fairly uniform lighting about 25% brighter than a sighted norm, and warns that strong directional light casts shadows which mask the contrast you designed, and that big swings in level defeat an eye that adapts slowly.
These are floors, not targets
Everything above is a legal minimum. Meeting it exactly buys a sign that a stranger, in a hurry, in bad light, can just read. TfL's standard runs the calculation in the more useful direction — pick a cap height, read off the maximum distance at which average eyesight can manage it, its eight standard sizes spanning roughly 6 to 60 metres — and instructs that the optimum size be used wherever possible, not the smallest legal one.
Common mistakes

"It's 5/8 inch, so it's compliant." Only under 6 feet of viewing distance at normal mounting height. Beyond that the minimum grows every single foot.
"Bolder is more legible." Above roughly 30% of cap height the counters fill in. There is a ceiling as well as a floor.
"The colours are very different." Different hue, not different lightness. Photocopy it in black and white, or desaturate the file: if the two tones merge, so does the sign.
"We checked it on screen." You checked a backlit, glare-free version at 40 cm. Print it at size, tape it to the actual wall, and stand where the counter puts you.
"Bigger is always safer." Panel area is finite, so bigger costs you destinations — and an oversized line steals attention from the one that matters. See Visual hierarchy.


Checking a sign in five steps

Stand at the nearest point you are physically allowed to reach. Measure that distance and the sign's height.
Compute the minimum cap height, then measure the actual letters. Most failures are here.
Check the stroke against the cap height: thinner than a tenth or thicker than a third is a problem.
Desaturate the colours in your head or on your phone. Does the text still separate from the plate?
Move your head. If a lamp or a window lands on the panel and the text disappears, the finish is wrong no matter what the numbers say.

              Five words the field uses interchangeably for five different things. Knowing which one you are looking at tells you what test it has to pass.
            
          
        
          
            
              Value structure
              How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.
            
          
        
          
            
              Visual hierarchy
              The order in which your eye visits the parts of an image — decided by the image, not by you.
